summary: Describes how to make DNSSEC NSEC records that cover a smaller range of names than RFC 4034 calls for. Generated and signed on demand, they let servers stop others from listing a zone's contents by walking the NSEC chain. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: In a signed DNS zone, each NSEC record lists the next name that really exists. A server that answers queries with these records can be asked repeatedly until it has handed out every name. This RFC makes those records cover as few names as possible, so the server signs a small record on demand each time it has to say that a name does not exist.

questions: how to prevent nsec zone walking
what is on-line signing in dnssec
subtitle: Small, on-demand NSEC records that stop a signed zone's names from being collected by walking the NSEC chain.

tldr.problem: An NSEC record names the next real name in a signed DNS zone, so repeated queries can reveal every name in the zone, even where zone transfers are forbidden.
tldr.mechanism: The server builds NSEC records that cover as few names as possible, and generates and signs them on demand when it has to deny that a name exists.
tldr.outcome: Walking a zone takes about as many queries as guessing every possible name. The price is that the server's private keys must be reachable online, and the RFC points to NSEC3 as a mechanism that avoids that.

facts.value: Add a leading label with a single null octet

today: RFC 4470 is a Proposed Standard from April 2006 that updates RFC 4034 and RFC 4035. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself points to NSEC3 as a mechanism then under development that avoids on-line signing.

sections.title: How NSEC Records Reveal a Zone
sections.content:
With DNSSEC, an NSEC record lists the next instantiated name in its zone, proving that no names exist in the span between the NSEC's owner name and the name in the next name field. In this document, an NSEC record is said to cover the names between its owner name and its next name.

Through repeated queries that return NSEC records, it is possible to retrieve all of the names in the zone, a process commonly called walking the zone. Some zone owners have policies forbidding zone transfers by arbitrary clients. This side effect of the NSEC architecture subverts those policies.

This document presents a way to prevent zone walking by constructing NSEC records that cover fewer names. Such records can make zone walking take approximately as many queries as simply asking for all possible names in a zone, which makes walking impractical. Some of these records must be created and signed on demand, which requires on-line private keys.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed DNS zone contains a record for each name that lists the next name that really exists. Ask the server for those records one after another and you can collect the whole list of names, even where the operator has forbidden zone transfers. This RFC shrinks the range each record covers, so collecting the list takes about as much work as guessing every possible name.

sections.title: When This Technique Applies
sections.content:
The technique may be useful to a zone owner that wants to use DNSSEC, is concerned about exposure of its zone contents via zone walking, and is willing to bear the costs of on-line signing.

On-line signing has several security risks, including an increased likelihood of private keys being disclosed and an increased risk of denial of service attack.

At the time this document was published, the DNSEXT working group was actively working on a mechanism to prevent zone walking that does not require on-line signing, tentatively called NSEC3. The new mechanism is likely to expose slightly more information about the zone than this technique, such as the number of instantiated names, but it may be preferable to this technique.
sections.plainLanguage: This approach fits a zone owner who wants DNSSEC, wants to hide the zone's names, and accepts the risk of signing on the fly. The RFC also names an alternative, NSEC3, which was being worked on at the time and which avoids on-line signing while revealing slightly more, such as how many names exist.

sections.title: Minimally Covering NSEC Records
sections.content:
The mechanism involves changes to NSEC records for instantiated names, which can still be generated and signed in advance, as well as the on-demand generation and signing of new NSEC records whenever a name must be proven not to exist.

In the next name field of an instantiated name's NSEC record, the server lists any name that falls lexically after the NSEC's owner name and before the next instantiated name in the zone, according to the ordering function in RFC 4034. This relaxes the requirement in section 4.1.1 of RFC 4034 that the next name field contains the next owner name in the zone. The change is expected to be fully compatible with all existing DNSSEC validators. These NSEC records are returned whenever proving something specific about the owner name, for example that no resource records of a given type appear at that name.

Whenever an NSEC record is needed to prove the non-existence of a name, a new NSEC record is produced and signed on demand. The new record has an owner name lexically before the queried name but lexically following any existing name, and a next name lexically following the queried name but before any existing name. The generated record's type bitmap must have the RRSIG and NSEC bits set, and should not have any other bits set, which relaxes the requirement in section 2.3 of RFC 4035 that NSEC records do not appear at names that did not exist before the zone was signed.

The functions that generate the lexically following and preceding names need not be perfect or consistent, but the generated NSEC records must not cover any existing names. The technique works best when they cover as few names as possible. This document calls these functions epsilon functions, a reference to the mathematical convention of using the Greek letter epsilon to represent small deviations. An NSEC record denying the existence of a wildcard may be generated in the same way; since the record covering a non-existent wildcard is likely to be used in response to many queries, a server may want to pregenerate or cache that record and its corresponding RRSIG.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of record are involved. Records for names that really exist are signed in advance as usual, but their next-name field may name any name that sorts between the owner name and the next real name. Records that deny a name are built and signed at the moment they are needed. The functions that pick the neighbouring names do not have to be perfect, but the record they produce must never cover a name that does exist.

sections.title: Two Records That Deny a Name
sections.content:
A query for an A record at the non-instantiated name example.com might produce two NSEC records: the first denying the existence of the name example.com, and the second denying the existence of a wildcard.

Before answering a query with such records, an authoritative server must test for the existence of names between these endpoints. If the generated NSEC would cover existing names, for example exampldd.com or *bizarre.example.com, a better epsilon function may be used, or the covered name closest to the queried name could be used as the NSEC owner name or next name, as appropriate. If an existing name is used as the NSEC owner name, that name's real NSEC record must be returned. Assuming an exampldd.com delegation exists, the record returned from the parent would then name exampldd.com and list the same next name, with the NS, DS, RRSIG and NSEC types.

Like every authoritative record in the zone, each generated NSEC record must have corresponding RRSIGs generated using each algorithm, but not necessarily each DNSKEY, in the zone's DNSKEY RRset, as described in section 2.2 of RFC 4035. To minimize the number of signatures that must be generated, a zone may wish to limit the number of algorithms in its DNSKEY RRset.
sections.plainLanguage: To deny that example.com exists, the server returns two records: one that denies the name itself, and one that denies a wildcard. The server first checks that no real name lies between the two ends of the record. If one does, it uses that real name as an endpoint instead, and returns that name's own record in the case where the real name is the owner.

sections.title: Epsilon Functions
sections.content:
Section 6.1 of RFC 4034 defines a strict ordering of DNS names. Working backward from that definition, it should be possible to define epsilon functions that generate the immediately following and preceding names. This document does not define such functions. Instead, it presents functions that come reasonably close to the perfect ones, and the server should still ensure that no generated NSEC covers any existing name.

To increment a name, add a leading label with a single null, zero-value, octet. To decrement a name, decrement the last character of the leftmost label, then fill that label to a length of 63 octets with octets of value 255. To decrement a null, zero-value, octet, remove the octet; if an empty label is left, remove the label. Defined numerically, the decrement function fills the leftmost label to its maximum length with zeros, numeric zeros rather than ASCII zeros, and subtracts one.

Both functions are imperfect: they do not take into account constraints on the number of labels in a name or on the total length of a name. The technique does not depend on perfect epsilon functions. It is sufficient to test whether any instantiated names fall into the span covered by the generated NSEC and, if so, substitute those instantiated owner names for the NSEC owner name or next name, as appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: An epsilon function finds a name just before or just after a given one. To move a name up, the RFC adds a label holding one zero byte. To move it down, it lowers the last character of the first label and fills that label with 63 bytes of value 255. These functions do not respect limits on label count or total length, so the server checks the result against the real names in the zone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This approach requires on-demand generation of RRSIG records, which creates several new vulnerabilities. First, on-demand signing requires that a zone's authoritative servers have access to its private keys, and storing private keys on well-known Internet-accessible servers may make them more vulnerable to unintended disclosure. Second, since generation of digital signatures tends to be computationally demanding, the requirement for on-demand signing makes authoritative servers vulnerable to a denial of service attack. Last, if the epsilon functions are predictable, on-demand signing may enable a chosen-plaintext attack on a zone's private keys. Zones using this approach should attempt to use cryptographic algorithms that are resistant to chosen-plaintext attacks. DNSSEC has a mandatory-to-implement algorithm, but that is a requirement on resolvers and validators; there is no requirement that a zone be signed with any given algorithm.

The success of the technique depends greatly on the quality of the epsilon functions chosen. An increment function that chooses a name obviously derived from the next instantiated name may be easily reverse engineered, destroying the value of the technique, and an increment function that always returns a name close to the next instantiated name is likewise a poor choice. Good choices are the ones that produce the immediately following and preceding names, though zone administrators may wish to use less perfect functions that return more human-friendly names.

Another obvious but misguided concern is the danger of synthesized NSEC records being replayed. An attacker could replay an old but still validly signed NSEC record after a new name has been added in the span covered by that record, incorrectly proving that there is no record at that name. This danger exists with DNSSEC as defined in RFC 4035. The techniques described here actually decrease the danger, since the span covered by any NSEC record is smaller than before, and choosing better epsilon functions further reduces it.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing on demand puts the private keys on servers that anyone can reach, and every signature takes computing power, so an attacker can either try to steal the keys or flood the server with work. The neighbouring-name functions must also be unpredictable, because a predictable function lets an attacker choose the text that gets signed. Replaying an old record is a smaller problem here than in plain DNSSEC, because the range each record covers is smaller.
